$comment: Item archetypes (PLAN §7): civilization x archetype x tier x affixes x provenance. 'fact' is real and per civilization; 'fiction' is the Anvil's line. They are separate fields and must stay in separate panels and typefaces on the client (non-negotiable 5). Hybrids carry no fact at all. Phase 0 names the three Cugnaux civilizations; the other twelve fall back to 'generic'.

fact.hallstatt: Long iron swords with decorated scabbards define the La Tène culture; Gaulish warriors of the Toulouse basin carried them.
fact.phoenicia: Leaf-shaped bronze blades circulated the Mediterranean with Phoenician trade in the early Iron Age.
fact.etruria: The kopis is a forward-curving single-edged blade shown in Etruscan and Greek art from the 6th century BCE.

archetypes.fiction: It cuts toward the ground, always.

names.hallstatt: Iron axe of the salt road

fact.hallstatt: Iron axes with wooden hafts survive from the Hallstatt salt mines, where brine preserved the wood.
fact.phoenicia: Bronze axe heads travelled as tools and as ingots in Phoenician cargoes.
fact.etruria: Charun's hammer is an attribute in Etruscan tomb painting, not a weapon found in graves.

fact.hallstatt: The carnyx was a bronze war trumpet held vertically, its bell shaped as a boar's head.
fact.phoenicia: The sign of Tanit appears on Carthaginian stelae from the 5th century BCE.
fact.etruria: The lituus, a curved augural staff, passed from Etruscan diviners to Roman priests.

archetypes.fiction: Point it at the ground and the ground answers.

fact.hallstatt: Iron Age shields were wood and leather with a metal boss; only the fittings survive in graves.
fact.phoenicia: Carved ivory plaques in Levantine style decorated furniture and fittings traded by Phoenician workshops.
fact.etruria: Etruscan bronze mirrors, engraved with myths on the back, were placed in women's tombs by the thousand.

archetypes.fiction: What it reflects is a little behind you.

fact.hallstatt: Sheet-bronze cauldrons were feasting and votive vessels across the Hallstatt and La Tène world.
fact.phoenicia: Purple dye was worked in vats and jars beside the sea; shell middens mark the dye works.
fact.etruria: Bucchero is the glossy black pottery of Etruria, 7th to 5th century BCE; the kantharos is its two-handled cup.

fact.hallstatt: Wool twills in checks and stripes survive from the Hallstatt salt mines, the oldest tartan-like textiles in Europe.
fact.phoenicia: Tyrian purple was the most expensive dye of antiquity, worth more than its weight in gold.
fact.etruria: The linen corselet was the light armour of Etruscan and Greek warriors.

archetypes.fiction: Warm on the side that faces down.

fact.hallstatt: Iron Age helmets with animal crests appear on the Gundestrup cauldron and in the Ciumești grave.
fact.phoenicia: Grimacing terracotta masks were placed in Carthaginian tombs, 7th to 5th century BCE.
fact.etruria: Negau-type bronze helmets, named for a hoard in Slovenia, were made in Etruria from the 5th century BCE.

archetypes.fiction: It fits. That is the worrying part.

fact.hallstatt: Gold torcs found at Fenouillet, Haute-Garonne, in 1841 are in the Musée Saint-Raymond, Toulouse; 3rd to 2nd century BCE.
fact.phoenicia: Core-formed glass pendant heads with striped beards were Phoenician trade goods, 6th to 3rd century BCE.
fact.etruria: The bulla is a lentoid pendant worn by Etruscan children and warriors; Rome adopted it.

names.hallstatt: Ingot of the gold of Tolosa

fact.hallstatt: The gold of Tolosa, sacred to the Tectosages, was seized by the consul Caepio in 106 BCE and lost; 'to have the gold of Tolosa' meant to be cursed.
fact.phoenicia: Levantine ivories, carved with sphinxes and palmettes, furnished palaces from Nimrud to Spain.
fact.etruria: The Piacenza liver, a 2nd-century BCE bronze model of a sheep's liver, is divided into regions named for gods.

hybrid_epithets.$comment: Hybrid names are dominant epithet plus dominant archetype name; PLAN §7 wants a written table per ordered pair, and for phase 0 the pair contributes the epithet. 'dominant>secondary'.

edibles.name: Cauldron broth
edibles.fact: Iron Age feasting centred on the cauldron; residues show meat and grain stews.

edibles.name: Salt of Salies
edibles.fact: Salies-du-Salat, Haute-Garonne, worked a salt spring from antiquity.

edibles.name: Isthmus wine
edibles.fact: Wine amphorae reached the Toulouse basin overland from the Mediterranean via the Aude.

edibles.name: Murex stew
edibles.fact: The dye snails were eaten too; middens hold both cracked and whole shells.

edibles.name: Banquet fig
edibles.fact: Figs, grapes and eggs appear on Etruscan banquet tables in tomb painting.
edibles.fiction: From a vintage not yet grown.
